# Why adding your child to the deed backfires

This is the most expensive piece of free advice in America, and it gets passed across kitchen tables constantly.

*Just add your daughter to the deed. Then when you pass, the house is hers and you skip probate.*

The first part is true. The house does go to her, and it does skip probate. That is exactly why the advice survives. It works, in the narrow sense that the thing you asked for happens.

It is what else happens that nobody mentions.

## Start with what a step up in basis actually is

Basis is what the tax code thinks you paid. When you sell, you owe tax on the difference between the sale price and your basis.

Say you bought the house in 1994 for $80,000, and today it is worth $400,000. Your basis is $80,000. Sell it yourself and there is $320,000 of gain to reckon with, though a good chunk of that may be sheltered if it is your primary residence.

Now here is the part that matters. **When you die, the basis of what you owned resets to the value on the date of death.** That is IRC 1014, and it is one of the most generous provisions in the whole code. Your daughter inherits the house with a basis of $400,000. She sells it the next month for $400,000 and owes tax on nothing at all. The entire thirty years of gain simply vanishes.

That is the step up, and it is worth real money.

## What the deed transfer does to it

When you add your daughter to the deed during your life, you have made her a **gift** of an interest in the house. Gifts do not get a step up. They get **carryover basis** under IRC 1015, which means she takes your old basis along with the property.

So her share carries a basis anchored in 1994 dollars. When she eventually sells, that gain is still there waiting, and she pays the tax on it.

You traded a probate proceeding, which is inconvenient and costs some money, for a tax bill that can be a large multiple of what probate would have cost. That trade is almost never worth it.

## And you handed her a legal exposure at the same time

Once her name is on the deed, she is an owner. Which means the house is now visible to everything in her life.

If she gets divorced, her interest in your house is on the table.

If she is sued, or has a business go badly, or a medical debt lands, a creditor with a judgment against her can attach her interest in the property you live in.

If she files bankruptcy, that interest is an asset.

None of that is theoretical. The house you have lived in for thirty years is now partly exposed to your child's life, and you cannot take it back without her cooperation.

## You also lost control

She is a co-owner now. You cannot sell without her signature. You cannot refinance without her signature. If she moves out of state, gets sick, stops speaking to a sibling, or simply says no, you are stuck.

And if she dies before you, her interest may pass to her spouse or her children rather than back to you, depending on how the deed reads.

## The North Carolina specifics

Two things worth knowing about how the deed itself has to read.

**Survivorship has to be spelled out.** In North Carolina, adding someone to a deed does not automatically create a right of survivorship. If the deed does not say so, you are tenants in common, each share passes under its own owner's will, and the probate you were trying to avoid happens anyway, just messier. Joint tenancy with right of survivorship is created under **NCGS 41-71**.

**If you are married, you may already have something better.** A married couple holding a home in North Carolina generally holds as **tenancy by the entirety** under NCGS 41-56. That gives survivorship at the first death **and** creditor protection, because a creditor of only one spouse generally cannot reach the property at all. Adding a child to that deed can break the entirety and give away the protection along with it.

## What people are usually actually trying to solve

Nearly always, the real goal is one of these.

**Avoid probate.** There are cleaner tools. A revocable trust holding title does it without a lifetime gift and without giving up the step up. Some states offer a transfer on death deed, and whether that fits here is worth asking about.

**Make sure a specific child gets the house.** A will or a trust does that, and it can be changed later if life changes. A deed cannot, not without that child's signature.

**Qualify for Medicaid.** This one worries me most. Transferring the house to a child to qualify for long term care generally triggers a penalty period that delays eligibility, and it forfeits the step up in the same move. It is the version of this mistake that costs the most and gets made under the most pressure. Talk to an elder law attorney before anyone signs anything.

## The one honest exception

Sometimes people do this deliberately, with a professional, because the numbers work for their particular situation. There are life estate deeds, including the enhanced version, that keep control and preserve the step up while still avoiding probate.

That is a different thing than what the neighbor suggested. The difference is that somebody ran the numbers first.

## Where I stop

I can explain why the step up matters and what a deed transfer costs you. I cannot tell you whether your family should retitle, what your current deed actually says, what a transfer you already made will cost, or how to undo one. Read your deed, then take it to a title attorney. If a transfer has already happened, take it to a CPA too, because the basis question is real and it does not go away by itself.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

# The form that beats your will

Most people spend real money on a will and never look at the form that overrides it.

If you are under sixty, the biggest thing you own is probably not your house. It is your 401(k), or your IRA, or a life insurance policy. And none of those pass under your will. They pass by contract, to whoever is written on a beneficiary form you filled out at a desk on your first day of a job you may not even have anymore.

The custodian pays the name on the form. That is the entire process. Your will is not consulted. Your executor cannot argue with it. A judge does not review it.

So the most valuable hour in estate planning is often not with a lawyer. It is you, logging into four accounts and reading what they say.

## The four ways this goes wrong

I want to be specific, because the failures are predictable and each one has a name.

### The ex spouse is still on it

This is the most common one, and it is the one people refuse to believe.

You divorce. The decree divides everything. In North Carolina, divorce revokes provisions for a former spouse in your **will**, under NCGS 31-5.4. That is real, and people hear it and assume the job is done.

It does nothing to your 401(k). Nothing to your IRA. Nothing to your life insurance. Those are contracts, and the contract still says her name.

I have seen this land on a second family years later, and there is usually nothing anyone can do about it. The paperwork was correct. It was just never updated.

### A child is named directly

Naming a minor feels like the obvious loving choice. It creates a problem instead.

A minor cannot legally receive and manage a large sum. So the money goes nowhere until a court appoints someone to hold it, which means a guardianship proceeding, which means lawyers and delay and court supervision, and then the money is handed over in full on the child's eighteenth birthday.

Eighteen. In one payment. To pay for whatever an eighteen year old decides to pay for.

### The estate is named as beneficiary

Sometimes the form says "my estate," either because someone chose it or because the space was left blank and the default kicked in.

That takes an asset that would have skipped probate entirely and drags it into probate. It becomes public, it waits behind creditors, and for a retirement account it can wreck the payout timeline, because an estate is not a person with a life expectancy.

### Nobody is named after the first person

Most forms have a primary line and a contingent line. People fill in the first and leave the second empty.

If your primary beneficiary dies before you, or with you, the empty line means the account defaults to whatever the plan document says. Which usually means your estate. Which means the paragraph above.

## The part that surprises people about inherited retirement accounts

Two more things worth knowing, because they change how much the money is actually worth.

**An inherited IRA does not get a step up in basis.** When you inherit stock or a house, the tax basis resets to the value at the date of death, and the built up gain disappears. A traditional retirement account does not work that way. It is income in respect of a decedent under IRC 691, and every dollar your beneficiary withdraws is taxable to them as ordinary income, exactly as it would have been to you.

So a $400,000 brokerage account and a $400,000 traditional IRA are not the same inheritance. Not close.

**And most beneficiaries now have ten years.** The old strategy of stretching withdrawals across a young beneficiary's lifetime is largely gone. Most people who inherit have to empty the account within ten years, and the 2024 final regulations added a requirement to take annual distributions during that window in some cases.

There are exceptions, and they matter. A surviving spouse. A minor child of the account owner. Someone disabled or chronically ill. Someone not more than ten years younger than the owner. Those beneficiaries still get life expectancy treatment. That disabled beneficiary exception connects directly to special needs planning, and it is a reason to be careful rather than a reason to relax.

## If you are married, the plan may already have an opinion

Workplace retirement plans governed by ERISA generally require your spouse to be the beneficiary unless your spouse consents in writing to someone else.

You cannot quietly name your brother. The plan will not let you, and if it did, the spouse would likely win anyway.

IRAs are different. There is no federal spousal consent requirement on an IRA, which surprises people who assume the rules are uniform.

## What to actually do this week

This costs nothing and takes about an hour.

1. List every account with a beneficiary line. Retirement plans from every employer, including the old ones. IRAs. Life insurance, including the small policy through work. Annuities. Any account with a transfer on death registration
2. Log in and read what each one says. Do not rely on memory and do not rely on what you filled out in 2011
3. Check the contingent line, not just the primary
4. Look for anyone who is deceased, divorced from you, a minor, or the word "estate"
5. Fix what needs fixing, then save the confirmation

Then do it again after any marriage, divorce, birth, or death in the family. Those four events are the ones that make a correct form wrong.

## Where I stop

I can tell you how these forms work and what commonly goes wrong on them. I cannot tell you who you should name, whether a trust belongs on that line, how to make a trust qualify so it does not collapse the payout period, or how to handle a designation that is already causing a problem. Those are planning decisions, and they belong with an attorney, especially if there is a blended family, a disabled beneficiary, or a large retirement balance involved.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

docs.body:
# No, your spouse does not automatically get everything

Ask ten married people in North Carolina what happens if they die without a will, and nine will tell you the same thing. *Everything goes to my husband.* Or my wife. It feels obvious. They built it together, so of course it stays with the one still standing.

It is not what the statute says, and the gap between those two things is where families come apart.

## What actually happens

When someone dies without a will, the state supplies one. It is called intestate succession, it lives in Chapter 29, and it does not know anything about your family. It applies a formula.

Here is the formula for the surviving spouse, straight from NCGS 29-14.

**Real property, meaning the house and the land:**

| If the person who died left | The spouse receives |
|---|---|
| One child, or the descendants of one deceased child | **one half** |
| Two or more children, or their descendants | **one third** |
| No children, but a surviving parent | **one half** |
| No children and no surviving parent | **all of it** |

**Personal property, meaning bank accounts, vehicles, investments, everything else:**

| If the person who died left | The spouse receives |
|---|---|
| One child or their descendants | the first **$60,000**, plus **half** the balance |
| Two or more children or their descendants | the first **$60,000**, plus **one third** of the balance |

If the personal property does not exceed $60,000 in total, the spouse takes all of it.

Read the first row of the first table again. If you are married with one child and you die without a will, **your spouse owns half the house and your child owns the other half.**

## Why that is worse than it sounds

If your child is an adult who loves your spouse, this is awkward and probably survivable.

If your child is a minor, your spouse now co-owns the house with a child who cannot legally sign anything, which usually means a court has to get involved to do almost anything with the property.

And if this is a **second marriage**, which is where I have seen the most damage, your spouse now co-owns the home with your children from the first marriage. People who may not like each other. People who may want very different things. Your spouse wants to keep living there. Your children own half and would like their half.

Nobody in that room is a villain. The statute simply did not know they were not a family, and it split the house between them.

## Three other rules worth knowing

**The year's allowance.** A surviving spouse can claim **$60,000** for support ahead of creditors, and eligible children can claim **$10,000** each. That is NCGS 30-15 and 30-17, and it is applied for on form AOC-E-100. It is cash reaching a grieving family early, and it is missed constantly because nobody tells them it exists.

**You cannot fully disinherit a spouse, even with a will.** North Carolina gives a surviving spouse the right to elect against the will and take a share anyway, and the share grows with the length of the marriage. From NCGS 30-3.1:

| Married for | Elective share |
|---|---|
| Less than 5 years | 15% |
| 5 to less than 10 years | 25% |
| 10 to less than 15 years | 33% |
| 15 years or more | 50% |

Very few people know it is a sliding scale. It is also the honest answer to why premarital agreements exist, because the waiver of this right lives at NCGS 30-3.6.

**A lot of property never reaches this formula at all.** Chapter 29 only governs probate property. If the house is held with survivorship, it goes to the survivor before intestacy is ever consulted. If a retirement account names a beneficiary, that beneficiary is paid. So the real answer for any given family depends on how things are titled, which is why titling comes first in everything I write.

## What a will actually buys you

Not much drama. A will simply lets you say who gets what, instead of accepting a formula written for the average of everyone.

If you are married with children, and especially if either of you has children from another relationship, the distance between what you assume and what the statute does is enormous. That distance is the entire case for a will, and it costs a fraction of what sorting out the alternative costs.

## Where I stop

I can show you the formula and explain what it does. I cannot apply it to your family, tell you what your estate would actually look like, advise anyone on whether to elect against a will, or compute the numbers behind an elective share claim. Those need an attorney, and if someone has already died without a will, that call should happen soon rather than eventually.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

# Someone died and you are the one handling it

Nobody prepares for this job. You get it because you were named in a document, or because you were the one who answered the phone.

Here is the shape of it, so at least the road is visible.

## First, the good news you probably have not heard

Two things are usually true and almost nobody knows them going in.

**Most of what they owned may never touch this process.** If the house was held with survivorship, it already belongs to the survivor. If the retirement account named a beneficiary, that person gets paid directly. If there was a funded trust, it is handled outside all of this. Probate reaches only what was in their name alone with nowhere else to go. For a lot of families that turns out to be a car and a checking account.

**There may be a shortcut.** North Carolina has a small estate affidavit for modest personal property estates, and a summary administration when the surviving spouse inherits everything. Either one skips most of what follows. Ask the Clerk about both before you start the long version.

## Where you go

The Clerk of Superior Court, in the county where the person actually lived. Not where they died, and not where the house is. If your mother lived in Cumberland County and died in a Raleigh hospital, you go to Cumberland.

The Clerk is the judge of probate here. There is no separate probate court, and for a straightforward estate you can often walk in and start.

Before you go, download **AOC-E-850**. It is the Clerk's own guide to this entire process, it is free, and it is written for you rather than for lawyers. Most people doing this job never learn it exists.

## Getting authority

You cannot do anything until the court says you can. Not close an account, not sell a car, not talk to the insurance company.

You apply on **AOC-E-201** if there is a will, or **AOC-E-202** if there is not. You take an oath on **AOC-E-400**. A bond may be required, on **AOC-E-401**, unless it is waived. Then the Clerk issues **letters** on **AOC-E-403**, and those letters are the thing every bank and brokerage will demand before they speak to you.

Two practical notes that save people a second trip. Bring the **original** will, not a copy. And order more certified copies of the letters than you think you need, because every institution keeps one and does not give it back.

## The clock you have to start

You publish a notice to creditors and mail it to the ones you know about. That opens a window during which claims can be presented.

This part feels like a formality and it is not. Claims get paid in an order the statute sets, and you do not get to choose. Paying the sympathetic creditor first, or paying anyone before the window closes, can make you personally responsible for it.

The hardest sentence I can offer here is this. Do not distribute anything to the family until the window has run, no matter how much pressure you are under. That pressure is real and it is always there, and giving in to it is how a well meaning person ends up owing money.

## The inventory

Within a deadline, you file a sworn list of what the person owned, valued as of the date they died, on **AOC-E-505**.

Get real values rather than guesses. Not because the Clerk is difficult, but because that date of death value becomes the tax basis for whoever inherits. A lazy number on this form can cost the family thousands later, when the house or the stock is sold.

If there is a safe deposit box, that is **AOC-E-520**.

## The allowance almost nobody claims

A surviving spouse can claim **$60,000** for support, ahead of creditors. Eligible children can claim **$10,000** each. It is form **AOC-E-100**.

This is cash reaching a grieving family early, and it is skipped constantly because no one mentions it. There is a deadline. Ask about it at the counter on your first visit.

## Taxes, which are not one thing

There are up to three separate filings and people are routinely surprised by the second and third.

The person's **final personal return** for their last year of life. Then, if the estate earns income while you are administering it, a **fiduciary income tax return**, federal Form 1041 and North Carolina Form D-407. A federal **estate tax return**, Form 706, is only required for very large estates, well above what most families have.

One thing worth knowing even for a small estate. If the surviving spouse might ever need the deceased spouse's unused exemption, that only transfers if a 706 is actually filed, even when no tax is owed. That is a conversation for a CPA or an attorney, and it is worth ten minutes of one.

## Accounting and finishing

You file accounts on **AOC-E-506**, annually while the estate is open and finally when it closes. The Clerk audits them against receipts.

So keep every receipt from day one. Not a shoebox. A folder, or a spreadsheet, with a note on what each payment was for. The single most common reason an estate drags on for an extra year is that nobody can document where the money went.

When the accounting is approved, the Clerk discharges you, and that discharge is the point of all of this. Until then, you are still carrying the responsibility.

## What this costs

Court costs run on the personal property in the estate, subject to a cap. You are also entitled to a commission for serving, within statutory limits, which many family members waive and are not obligated to.

The national averages you will find online are not North Carolina and are usually much higher than what this actually costs here.

## When to stop reading and call someone

Some of these are not do it yourself situations, and recognizing that early is cheaper than recognizing it late.

- Anyone is contesting the will, or threatening to
- The debts may exceed the assets
- There is a business, a farm, or property in another state
- Beneficiaries are not speaking to each other
- Anything about the paperwork does not match what you were told

## Where I stop

I can walk you through the shape of the process and what each form is for. I cannot tell you whether this estate qualifies for a shortcut, who should serve if the family disagrees, whether a particular claim has to be paid, what an unusual asset is worth, or what to do about a contested anything. Take those to an estate attorney, and take them early rather than after a deadline has passed.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

docs.body:
# The trust nobody funded

This is the most common failure in estate planning, and it happens to people who did everything they were told.

They paid an attorney. They signed a stack of documents. They got a handsome binder with a tab for every section. They put it on a shelf and felt, reasonably, that they had handled it.

Then they died, and the family found out the trust was empty.

## A trust is not the binder

The binder is instructions. The trust is a relationship, and it needs four things to exist. Someone who sets it up. Someone who runs it. Someone it benefits. And **property that is actually in it**.

North Carolina says this plainly at NCGS 36C-4-401 and 36C-4-402. A trust needs property.

Signing the document creates the container. It does not put anything inside. That second step is called **funding**, and it means going to each institution and changing the name on the account or the deed from you personally to you as trustee of your trust.

The house has to be deeded in. The brokerage account has to be retitled. The bank account has to be changed. Each one is a separate errand at a separate place, and none of them happen automatically because you signed something.

## What actually goes wrong

Say you set up a revocable trust so the family avoids probate. The lawyer prepares a new deed for the house, and you sign it. Good.

But you opened a brokerage account two years later and never thought about it. And you refinanced the house, and the lender wanted it out of the trust for the closing, and it was never deeded back in. And there is a rental property you bought after all of this that nobody ever mentioned.

Every one of those goes through probate. The exact thing you paid to avoid, happening to most of what you own, while an empty trust sits on the shelf doing nothing.

## The pourover will is a net, not a plan

Your attorney almost certainly also prepared a pourover will. It says anything not already in the trust should pour into it at death. North Carolina allows that at NCGS 31-47.

People hear this and relax. They should not.

**Anything the pourover will catches goes through probate first.** That is what a will does. The pourover is a safety net for the item you forgot, not a substitute for funding. A trust with a pourover will and nothing in it is a very expensive way to have an ordinary will.

## Two things a revocable trust actually does

Most people only know the first one.

**It avoids probate at death.** Property already titled to the trust does not pass through the court, so it moves privately and usually faster.

**It handles you while you are alive.** This is the half nobody talks about, and I think it is the more valuable half. If you have a stroke tomorrow, your successor trustee steps in and manages what the trust holds. No court, no guardianship, no hearing where a judge decides whether you can manage your own affairs.

That second job only works on funded assets too. An empty trust cannot manage anything.

## What it does not do

A revocable trust does not protect your assets from your creditors. Not in North Carolina, not anywhere, and the statute says so directly. **NCGS 36C-5-505** provides that a creditor can reach the maximum amount that could be distributed to you. Since a revocable trust is entirely available to you, it is entirely available to them.

The word people hear is "trust" and they assume armor. Revocable means you kept control, and keeping control means keeping the exposure. That is the trade, and it is a fair one, but it should be understood.

A revocable trust also does not save income tax while you are alive. You still report everything on your own return.

## The funding checklist

If you have a trust, this is the afternoon that makes it real.

**Retitle these:** real estate by recorded deed, bank and brokerage accounts, business interests, and any valuable personal property held in your name alone.

**Do not simply retitle these:** retirement accounts. Naming a trust on an IRA or a 401(k) has real tax consequences and can collapse the payout period for your beneficiaries. Sometimes it is exactly right, especially where a beneficiary is disabled or too young. It is never a do it yourself decision. Ask before you touch it.

**Ask about this one:** if you are married and own your home as tenancy by the entirety, that titling carries creditor protection a trust does not have. Deeding it into a trust can give that up. There are ways to handle it. Raise it specifically.

**Then keep doing it.** Every new account, every property purchased after the trust was signed, has to be titled correctly at the time. The classic miss is the asset acquired after the plan was finished.

## How to check yours tonight

Pull the binder. Then pull a recent statement for every account you own and the deed to your house.

Read the name on each one. If it says your name alone, that asset is not in the trust, whatever the binder says.

Make the list of what is out. That list is your next conversation, and it is a short one for the attorney who set it up.

## Where I stop

I can explain what funding is and why it decides whether any of this works. I cannot tell you whether a revocable trust suits your family, which of your assets belong in it, how to handle an entirety property without losing the creditor protection, or whether a trust should be named on your retirement account. That last one especially. Take the list to the attorney who drafted it, and if they did not walk you through funding the first time, that itself is worth noticing.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

# The four documents that keep your family out of court

Estate planning gets sold as what happens after you die. The part that is far more likely to affect you is what happens if you are still here and cannot speak for yourself.

A stroke. A bad fall. A diagnosis that moves faster than anyone expected. In that moment your family discovers something that shocks them every single time.

**Being family does not give them authority.** Your wife cannot sell your car if the title is in your name. Your son cannot access your bank account to pay your mortgage. The hospital may talk to them or may not. Love is not a legal document, and the bank does not care how long you have been married.

Without paperwork, the only remaining path is guardianship, which means going to court to ask a judge to declare you incapable of managing your own life. That is Chapter 35A, and it is public, slow, expensive, and permanent in practice.

All four of the documents below exist to make that unnecessary.

## 1. The durable power of attorney, for your money

This names someone to handle property and finances if you cannot. Pay the mortgage, deal with insurance, manage accounts, sell a car, talk to the IRS.

North Carolina's Uniform Power of Attorney Act is Chapter 32C, and one detail there is worth knowing. Under **NCGS 32C-1-104**, a power of attorney in North Carolina is **durable by default**. It survives your incapacity unless the document says otherwise. That reverses the old rule, where you had to say so explicitly, and it is a good default.

Two things people get wrong.

**The springing power.** Some documents say the agent's authority only begins once a doctor certifies you are incapacitated. It sounds careful. In practice it means your family is chasing a physician's letter during the worst week of their lives, while the mortgage is due. Many attorneys now recommend against it. Ask about the tradeoff rather than assuming one answer.

**The hot powers.** Certain authorities, including the power to make gifts, are not implied and have to be granted expressly. This matters a great deal if long term care planning may ever be needed, because an agent without gifting authority cannot do it.

There is also a provision worth appreciating. **NCGS 32C-1-119** deals with acceptance of and reliance on a power of attorney, and it exists because banks used to refuse perfectly valid documents. The statute now provides for reliance and creates consequences for unreasonable refusal.

## 2. The health care power of attorney, for your body

This names someone to make medical decisions when you cannot make them yourself. Chapter 32A, Article 3, at NCGS 32A-15 through 32A-27.

Your agent talks to doctors, consents to or refuses treatment, chooses facilities, and gets access to your records. **NCGS 32A-19** sets the extent of that authority and what limits you can place on it.

Pick the person who can hold steady in a hospital hallway and say what you would have said. That is not always the oldest child, and it is not always your spouse. Name a backup too.

## 3. The living will, for the end

This one is a different document in a different chapter, and people conflate the two constantly.

The living will is the **Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death**, and it lives at **NCGS 90-321**, in Article 23 of Chapter 90, not in Chapter 32A with the health care power.

The difference matters. Your health care agent speaks for you across the whole range of medical decisions. The living will is you speaking directly, in advance, about whether you want life prolonging measures in specific end stage circumstances.

They work together. The living will tells your agent what you wanted, so the hardest decision of their life is not also a guess.

## 4. The HIPAA authorization, which makes the others usable

The smallest document and the one most often left out.

Federal privacy law prevents providers from sharing your medical information without authorization. Your agent can be perfectly appointed and still be told nothing over the phone at two in the morning.

A HIPAA authorization solves it. It is short, it is cheap, and without it the other three run into a wall at the exact moment they are needed.

## What happens if you skip them

Chapter 35A, and it is worth seeing plainly.

Someone files a petition with the Clerk. You are entitled to counsel or a guardian ad litem under **NCGS 35A-1107**. You have a **right to a jury** under 35A-1110. There is a hearing, possibly a multidisciplinary evaluation, and then an adjudication order under 35A-1112 that determines whether you can manage your own affairs.

If a guardian is appointed, they file accountings with the court, sometimes for years. Your family ends up in a courthouse instead of a kitchen, and the person they are talking about is sitting in the room.

Everything above costs a fraction of that and takes an afternoon.

## The practical part

Sign all four at once, because they cover different things and each has a gap the others fill. Name backups on every one, since the person you name may be unavailable or may be in the car with you.

Then, and this is the step people skip, **give copies to the people who need them**. Your agent needs the originals or certified copies. Your doctor should have the health care documents on file. A document nobody can find at 2 a.m. is the same as no document.

Revisit after any divorce, death, or falling out. An agent you no longer trust is worse than no agent named at all.

## Where I stop

I can explain what each document does and why the set works together. I cannot tell you which powers to grant, who should serve as your agent, whether a springing power fits your situation, or what any of these should say. And if someone in your family has already lost capacity without these in place, that is a guardianship question and it needs an attorney now rather than later.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

# What happens if you leave money to someone on disability

Here is a question I get asked in a quiet voice, usually after everything else has been settled.

*My son has a disability. He gets benefits. If I leave him money, does he lose them?*

The honest answer is that he might, and it is one of the few places in planning where doing the kind thing the obvious way causes real harm.

## Why the money is the problem

Some benefits are means tested. That means the government looks at what the person owns before it pays. Supplemental Security Income and Medicaid both work this way, and both carry asset limits that are low. Not low as in modest. Low as in a few thousand dollars.

So when an inheritance lands in that person's name, the math changes overnight. They are suddenly over the limit. The benefits stop. And the benefits were not pocket money. They were paying for housing, for a caregiver, for therapies, for the medical coverage that no private plan will replace at any price he can afford.

The family meant to help. What actually happened is that a modest inheritance bought a few months of expenses and cost a lifetime of support.

That is the whole problem in one paragraph, and almost nobody sees it coming.

## First, know which benefit you are talking about

This trips up more conversations than anything else, so it is worth thirty seconds.

**Supplemental Security Income** is need based. It looks at assets. This is the one that inheritance threatens.

**Social Security Disability Insurance** is different. It was earned through work history, yours or a parent's, and it does not care what the person owns. An inheritance does not touch it.

Many people receive both. Many families use the two names interchangeably and plan for the wrong one, which produces a confident answer that happens to be wrong. Find out which one before anyone decides anything.

## The fix is a container, not a smaller gift

The instinct is usually to leave less, or to leave the money to a sibling and ask them to take care of their brother. Both of those are worse than they sound. Leaving less still crosses the limit. Leaving it to a sibling means it is legally the sibling's money, exposed to the sibling's divorce, the sibling's creditors, and the sibling's own change of heart.

The actual answer is a trust built for this purpose. The money is there, it is spendable on your son's behalf, and it never belongs to him in the way the benefit rules count.

There are two versions, and which one you are in depends entirely on **whose money it was to begin with.**

## Third party: the one you want

This is the one you set up. It holds your money, or a grandparent's, for your son's benefit. The assets were never his, so the benefit rules never counted them.

The important part comes at the end. Because it was never his money, there is **no payback to Medicaid** when he dies. Whatever is left can go to his siblings, or wherever you say.

This is the planned version, and it is the one families should hear about first.

## First party: the rescue

Sometimes the money is already his. A personal injury settlement. An inheritance that arrived outright because nobody knew to plan for it. A grandmother who meant well.

There is a fix. Federal law carves out an exception at **42 U.S.C. 1396p(d)(4)(A)** for a trust holding the disabled person's own assets. There is also a pooled trust version at **(d)(4)(C)**, run by a nonprofit, which can make sense for smaller amounts.

The trade is real. Because it was his money, Medicaid gets paid back from whatever remains when he dies. That is the price of the rescue, and it is usually far better than the alternative.

If money has already landed, this is not hopeless. It is urgent, but it is not hopeless.

## The mistake that undoes everything

You can do all of this correctly and still have it fail, and here is how.

You set up the trust. You name it in your will. Everything is right. Then your mother writes her own will, thinks of her grandson, and leaves him ten thousand dollars directly. Or an aunt names him on a life insurance policy. Or someone lists him as a beneficiary on an IRA.

None of those go through your will. None of them touch your trust. The money lands in his name and the whole structure fails.

**So the real work is the phone calls.** Everyone in the family who might leave him something needs to know that the gift goes to the trust and not to him. Grandparents. Aunts and uncles. Godparents. It feels awkward to raise. It is the single most important thing on this page.

## Why one paragraph decides everything

Two trusts can hold the same money for the same person and produce opposite results, based on the language describing when the trustee may spend.

If the trust says the trustee **shall** provide for support and maintenance, that can be treated as money the person is entitled to, which makes it an available resource, which defeats the purpose entirely.

If the trustee has **absolute discretion** and the trust is written to supplement rather than replace what the government provides, it behaves the way it should.

North Carolina addresses this directly at **NCGS 36C-5-504**, which deals with discretionary trusts and the effect of a standard. This is why a special needs trust is not a form you download. The paragraph that looks like boilerplate is the entire product.

## ABLE accounts, for the everyday money

There is one more tool worth knowing, and it is the one that gives your son some dignity.

An **ABLE account** under **IRC 529A** lets a person whose disability began before a set age hold money in their **own name**, under their own control, without it counting against the SSI resource limit, up to a ceiling. He can have a debit card. He can buy his own things.

Most families use an ABLE account alongside a trust rather than instead of one. The trust holds the serious money. The account holds his money.

## The document nobody requires and every family needs

Write a letter of intent.

It is not legal. No statute mentions it. No lawyer will draft it for you.

It is you, writing down how your son takes his coffee. What his mornings look like. Which noises frighten him and which ones he loves. What his last three doctors figured out that is not in any chart. Who his friends are. What he is proud of.

The trust handles the money. This handles the person, for whoever steps in when you cannot.

In my experience it is the piece families put off the longest and the piece they are most grateful to have.

## What to take to a lawyer

You do not need to arrive with answers. You need to arrive with the right questions.

- Which benefits does he actually receive, SSI or SSDI or both
- Are we planning ahead, or is there money already in his name
- Who else in the family might leave him something, and have they been told
- Who should be trustee after we are gone, and who after that
- Does an ABLE account make sense alongside the trust
- Is there a pooled trust option worth comparing

This is genuinely a specialty. A general estate planning attorney may do fine work and still miss the benefits interaction. Ask directly whether they handle special needs planning.

## Where I stop

I can explain how these pieces work and why they exist. I cannot tell you whether a particular gift would cost a particular person their benefits, which trust fits your family, how to repair an inheritance that already arrived, or what the trust should say. Those need a lawyer who does this work, and they need one before anybody signs anything or moves any money.

*Educational reference. I am not an attorney and I am not a registered investment adviser. Nothing here is legal, tax, or investment advice.*

# What Kristian thinks about titling, basis and how assets are held

Written by the house from every document he has on this theme. It carries no figures of its own by design: the sources carry the numbers and the live registers carry the current ones.

## The position

**Property transferred by gift during life carries the donor's old basis forward; property inherited at death gets basis reset to date of death value, and that difference is usually worth more than what probate costs.** This claim rests on "Why adding your child to the deed backfires" and is tied directly to IRC 1014 and IRC 1015. The step up at death is the single most valuable tax rule in routine estate planning, and lifetime transfers forfeit it.

**Adding a co-owner to a deed during life exposes the property to that person's creditors, divorces, and judgments, and you cannot reverse it without their signature.** From "Why adding your child to the deed backfires." Once someone is an owner, their life attaches to the property, and control is shared or lost.

**Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance override the will entirely, and outdated or missing designations are the most common way an estate plan fails in practice.** This is the central claim in "The form that beats your will" and connects to ERISA spousal consent rules and state law limits on will revocation by divorce. The contract pays the name on the form, regardless of what any will or divorce decree says.

**Naming a minor directly as beneficiary creates a court supervised guardianship and a lump sum distribution at age eighteen, both of which are avoidable problems.** From "The form that beats your will." The instinct to name a child directly is common and produces the exact outcome no parent wants.

**Inherited retirement accounts do not receive a step up in basis and most non spouse beneficiaries now face a ten year payout window with required annual distributions in some cases.** From "The form that beats your will," tracing to IRC 691 and the final regulations under IRC 401(a)(9). An inherited IRA is taxable income, not tax free inheritance, and the timeline is compressed for most people.

**In North Carolina, survivorship must be explicitly stated in a deed or it does not exist, and tenancy by the entirety offers creditor protection that adding a third person can destroy.** From "Why adding your child to the deed backfives," grounded in NCGS 41-71 and NCGS 41-56. The state does not assume survivorship, and married couples often hold something better than they realize.

## How he gets there

He starts with the tax consequence and makes it concrete with an example anchored in real dollar amounts across a plausible time span. A house bought in 1994 for one figure and worth another today. The gain is named, the step up is measured, and the lifetime transfer is compared directly to the inheritance alternative. He does not argue in the abstract about basis; he shows what it costs.

He treats the legal exposure as equal weight to the tax cost, not secondary. Creditors, divorce, bankruptcy, and loss of control are named as events that happen, not as remote risks, and he does not soften them. The house you live in is now visible to your child's life, full stop.

He refuses to let a mechanical success hide a structural failure. The deed does transfer, probate is avoided, the thing people wanted happens, and that is exactly why the advice survives and exactly why it is wrong. He separates what people ask for from what they actually need.

He checks what the document says, not what someone remembers filling out. Log in and read the form. Read the contingent line. Check after every marriage, divorce, birth, or death. This is the operational discipline under everything: the paper controls, memory does not, and outdated paper is the most common point of failure.

He names the exception and distinguishes it from the mistake. There are life estate deeds, including enhanced versions, that preserve control and the step up while avoiding probate. That is not what the neighbor suggested, and the difference is that someone ran the numbers first. He will not let the existence of a correct version excuse the common wrong one.

## Where he has repeated himself

The step up in basis at death is now the weight bearing concept across both documents. It is the reason adding a child to the deed backfires and the reason an inherited IRA is not equivalent to an inherited brokerage account. The mechanics are explained twice, from different entry points, both times treating it as underappreciated rather than widely understood.

The gap between what people think estate planning is and where the plan actually lives. One document focuses on deeds, the other on beneficiary forms, but both make the same structural point: the expensive professionally drafted will is sitting next to an informal decision that overrides it. The kitchen table advice, the form from the first day of an old job. That is where the plan fails.

Control and exposure as a package. Once someone else is named on something, you lose control and they gain exposure. This is true of a deed with a co-owner and true of a beneficiary designation naming a minor. Different assets, same structural problem, and he has now circled it twice.

The unwritten piece is probably about revocable trusts as the alternative that solves multiple problems at once. He has now said twice that there are better tools, named the trust in passing both times, and not yet explained how it actually operates or when the cost is worth it. That would be the natural next document.

## Tension and contradiction

In "Why adding your child to the deed backfires," he writes that tenancy by the entirety "gives survivorship at the first death and creditor protection, because a creditor of only one spouse generally cannot reach the property at all." That creditor protection is stated as the norm.

But the word "generally" is doing real work there, and the second document does not return to explain when it fails. If a creditor of one spouse cannot generally reach entirety property, that implies sometimes they can, and the line between general and exception is not drawn. The two documents do not contradict each other, but the first one opens a question the second one does not answer.

## What is unsettled

The role of state law variation in beneficiary designation outcomes. He notes that North Carolina divorce law revokes will provisions for a former spouse but does nothing to a 401(k), and he notes that IRAs do not have a federal spousal consent requirement while ERISA plans do. But he has not said whether North Carolina or any other state imposes its own rules on IRA beneficiary forms, or whether some states give a surviving spouse a claim against a designation that names someone else. The general principle is clear; the state by state boundary is not.

The mechanics of how a trust qualifies as a designated beneficiary for the stretch. He says in "The form that beats your will" that making a trust qualify so it does not collapse the payout period is a planning decision that belongs with an attorney. He has flagged the issue but not explained what the qualification rules actually require, which means a reader knows the risk exists but cannot assess whether their own trust clears it.

What happens when an outdated beneficiary designation is discovered after the account owner has died. Both documents describe the problem but neither walks through the fight. Can an ex spouse be displaced after the fact? What does a court actually do when the will says one thing and the IRA says another? He stops at "the custodian pays the name on the form," which is the rule, but there are presumably cases that test it and he has not said what those look like.

The difference between transfer on death deeds and life estate deeds, and which one he thinks is better in North Carolina. He mentions both in passing, calls the life estate deed with enhancement the "one honest exception," but does not compare them directly. A reader knows both exist and both might avoid probate without forfeiting the step up, but does not know when to use which.

## Where this stops

This is explanation of the structure and the common mistakes, not a decision about what your deed should say or who belongs on your beneficiary form. He will tell you why the step up matters, what a deed transfer costs, and what happens when a designation is wrong. He will not tell you whether your family should retitle, what your current deed actually says, what a transfer you already made will cost you, or how to undo one that has already happened.

He will not tell you who you should name, whether a trust belongs on a beneficiary line, or how to make a trust qualify for stretch treatment. He will not tell you whether your particular IRA custodian or your particular employer plan has rules that differ from the federal baseline. He will not run the numbers on whether a life estate deed makes sense for your situation.

Read your deed, take it to a title attorney. If a transfer has already happened, take it to a CPA. If there is a blended family, a disabled beneficiary, or a large retirement balance, the beneficiary question belongs with an attorney. Those are planning decisions, not explanations, and planning is where he stops.

# What Kristian thinks about charitable planning

Written by the house from every document he has on this theme. It carries no figures of its own by design: the sources carry the numbers and the live registers carry the current ones.

## The position

Charitable remainder trusts remain among the most useful instruments in wealth transfer when the charity genuinely comes first, but the IRS has now drawn an unmistakable line between planning and disguise. That claim rests on *When a Charitable Trust Becomes a Shelter: The IRS Draws a Line on CRATs* and *When Silence Becomes the Violation: The IRS Lists Abusive CRAT Transactions*, which cover the same regulatory action from two angles: one focused on the advisor's new disclosure burden, the other on the mechanics of the abusive structure itself.

A CRAT that puts the charity first has nothing to hide on a disclosure form. The trusts that suddenly look nervous when a reporting box appears are answering the question about their own purpose more honestly than any brochure could. That claim appears in both sources and is the through line: the disclosure requirement separates legitimate charitable planning from structures that only wear the costume.

The specific pattern the IRS named a listed transaction involves transferring appreciated property into a purported CRAT, selling it inside the trust, using the proceeds to buy a single premium immediate annuity, and then claiming the annuity payments back to the donor are taxable only under section 72 while the capital gain on the original sale vanishes under section 664 treatment. That is not charitable planning but a sale dressed as a gift, engineered so the tax on the sale never appears. Both sources describe this mechanism, with *When Silence Becomes the Violation* providing the statutory citations.

Material advisors and participants now carry an affirmative duty to disclose these structures, and the penalties for skipping that disclosure are severe. Reporting failures in this regime run into six figures per lapse, and the penalties attach to the non-disclosure itself, independent of whether the underlying position is ever disallowed. That claim is supported by both sources, with *When a Charitable Trust Becomes a Shelter* emphasizing that "I didn't know I had to file" is not a defense.

The IRS is not attacking legitimate charitable remainder trusts. It is drawing a bright line between planning and laundering, and asking advisors to stand on the right side of it in writing. A legitimate CRAT uses the trust to unwind a concentrated position with less tax drag, provides income for life, and leaves a genuine gift at the end. Both sources affirm this distinction and point to the Wealth Guide for coverage of honest versions.

For a fiduciary, the disclosure line was never a burden but always the job. A trustee's signature should never be the quietest part of a transaction. That claim appears in both sources as the fiduciary read: duty is the point, and silence is now the violation, not the strategy.

## How he gets there

He starts with the structure itself, naming the statutes and describing the sequence of transactions that creates the abuse. He does not rely on IRS characterization alone but walks through the mechanics so the reader can see what makes the scheme a disguise rather than a plan. The appreciated property transfer, the trust sale, the single premium annuity purchase, and the misapplication of sections 72 and 664 are all named in order. That precision is the foundation: if you cannot describe what the structure does, you cannot separate legitimate planning from costume.

He treats the disclosure requirement as diagnostic rather than punitive. A structure that fears the paperwork is revealing its own purpose. He refuses to frame the reporting obligation as regulatory overreach or as mere compliance theater. Instead, he asks what a legitimate trust would have to hide on a disclosure form, and the answer is nothing. The requirement separates trusts that are genuinely charitable from trusts that only appear so, and that separation is worth the friction.

He uses the fiduciary lens as the decisive test. Not what is legal, not what is disclosed, but what a fiduciary could administer without the signature becoming the quietest part of the transaction. The question is not whether the IRS will catch it but whether the advisor could stand publicly on the right side of the line the disclosure form draws. That is the filter: duty first, then structure.

He gives the legitimate version its own paragraph in both pieces, naming the honest use case for a charitable remainder trust and pointing to where he has covered it in full. He does this to hold the ground: the IRS action does not taint the instrument, it isolates the abuse. The through line is that planning and disguise are not close calls, and the people who cannot tell the difference are the people who should not be designing these trusts.

## Where he has repeated himself

He has now written twice on the same regulatory action, once focused on the advisor's disclosure burden and once on the abusive structure itself, and both pieces end at the same fiduciary checkpoint: silence is the violation, and a trustee's signature should never be the quietest part of a transaction. The repetition signals that the unwritten piece is about the advisor's exposure when the trust itself is legitimate but the numbers are optimistic or the remainder interest is implausibly small. He has drawn the line at outright disguise, but he has not yet written the piece on where honest planning shades into aggressive planning, and what the disclosure requirement does to structures that are not abusive but are not comfortable either.

He has twice pointed readers to the Wealth Guide for coverage of legitimate charitable remainder trusts, which means the substantive treatment of how to use a CRAT correctly lives elsewhere. The repetition suggests he sees these two pieces as warnings, not instructions, and the instructional content is already written and stable.

## Tension and contradiction

None found.

## What is unsettled

He has flagged the disclosure requirement as now mandatory for material advisors and participants, but he has not said what makes someone a material advisor in this context or how the IRS will enforce the disclosure obligation against advisors who were peripherally involved. The question of where the disclosure duty stops is open.

He has described the abusive structure as involving closely held business interests, but he has not said whether the listed transaction designation applies only to business interests or extends to other appreciated property such as publicly traded stock or real estate. The scope of the listing is not fully mapped.

He has stated that the penalties for non-disclosure run into six figures per lapse, but he has not cited the specific penalty provision or said whether the penalty is per trust, per year, or per transaction. The quantification of exposure is incomplete.

He has said that a legitimate CRAT has nothing to hide on a disclosure form, but he has not addressed what happens when a trust that was structured legitimately is later challenged on valuation or on the reasonableness of the remainder interest. The question of how disclosure affects litigation posture is unsettled.

## Where this stops

This is the boundary between regulatory classification and trust design. He has covered what makes a CRAT abusive and what the disclosure requirement now demands of advisors, but he has not covered how to design a charitable remainder trust from scratch, how to value the remainder interest, how to choose between a CRAT and a charitable remainder unitrust, or how to administer the trust once it is funded. A reader would still need counsel on the mechanics of creating and running a legitimate trust, on the tax reporting the trust itself must file annually, and on how to document the donor's charitable intent in a way that survives IRS scrutiny if the trust is ever examined.

# What Kristian thinks about trustee duty and fiduciary conduct

Written by the house from every document he has on this theme. It carries no figures of its own by design: the sources carry the numbers and the live registers carry the current ones.

## The position

A trustee's duty is already more demanding than the industry treats it. The statute gives remaindermen a present claim on information and transparency, not a future one that activates at distribution, but most corporate trustees discharge that duty at the floor by mailing an annual statement and calling it done. **The Relationship the Statute Already Requires** shows that under NCGS 36C-1-103 and 36C-8-813, remainder beneficiaries are qualified beneficiaries today, owed the trust instrument, holdings, and accountings on reasonable request, which means the law already assumes a relationship that most banks have never built.

The duty of impartiality between beneficiaries cannot be satisfied with unexamined defaults. Planning software that opens to age 90 or 95 for every client is not a conservative assumption; it is an outsourced allocation between the income beneficiary and the remaindermen, and **The Age Your Plan Assumes You Die** argues that NCGS 36C-9-902 and 36C-8-803 require the trustee to weigh distribution requirements specific to the actual beneficiary, not to accept a vendor's placeholder. A trustee entitled to conservatism is not entitled to conservatism by accident.

Control retained is protection forfeited. **The Wall That Didn't Hold** demonstrates that estate tax effectiveness and creditor or divorce protection are not the same test, and a trust labeled irrevocable but administered by a grantor who kept removal power over trustees and an investment advisory role can be treated as the grantor's asset when a court asks who really controls it. The [figure withheld: see the cited source and the live register] included in the marital estate in C.S. v. R.H. was in irrevocable trusts that the grantor never actually let go of. Protection is a function of genuine relinquishment, not of the word on the cover page.

A fiduciary duty is not conditioned on the account being lucrative. **Who Takes the Trust Nobody Gets Rich On?** names the pattern of trust companies exiting special needs work or pricing it beyond reach, and argues that the whole point of fiduciary designation is that someone answers for what belongs to a person who cannot fully answer for themselves. A special needs trust under 42 USC 1396p(d)(4)(A) only protects benefits if a human being actually administers it, and thin margins are not a basis to decline the trust nobody gets rich on.

Bad faith costs what you took, not what you can afford. **The Trustee Who Drained a Trust to [figure withheld: see the cited source and the live register]** explains California Probate Code section 859, which imposes a strict mandatory penalty of twice the value of property wrongfully taken in bad faith, with no mitigation for the wrongdoer's inability to pay. The Court of Appeal held in Moramarco v. Nowakoski that a penalty tethered to the size of the theft and gated by intent is proportionate by design, and deterrence does not bend to the bank balance of the person being deterred. A fiduciary answers for what he was trusted with, and the answer cannot be negotiated down to what is convenient after the fact.

A trust is not the binder and funding is not optional. **The trust nobody funded** walks through NCGS 36C-4-401 and 36C-4-402, which require property for a trust to exist, and explains that signing the document creates the container but does not put anything inside. Retitling each asset into the trust is a separate errand at each institution, none of them automatic, and a pourover will is a safety net for the forgotten asset, not a substitute for funding, because anything it catches goes through probate first.

## How he gets there

He reasons from the statute to the practice, not the other way around. When an industry norm conflicts with the plain language of a trust code section, he holds the statute as the rule and the norm as the thing that needs defending. He does this in **The Relationship the Statute Already Requires**, reading NCGS 36C-1-103 and 36C-8-813 to mean that remaindermen are owed information today, then measuring the one-page annual statement against that standard and finding it legally sufficient but relationally empty. The statute is not aspirational; it is the floor, and compliance measured against convenience rather than the beneficiary's actual need is compliance done wrong.

He checks what the beneficiary on the other side absorbs. A trustee choosing between two beneficiaries has to see the cost on both sides, and an unexamined assumption is an allocation someone still paid for. In **The Age Your Plan Assumes You Die**, he shows that a software default to age 95 for a beneficiary likely to live to 78 tilts the portfolio toward growth the income beneficiary will never see, and the remaindermen collect the difference. Reverse it and the corpus cannot sustain the distribution rate, and the remaindermen absorb the shortfall. Same number, opposite injury, both prohibited by the duty of impartiality, and a single paragraph in the file recording the estimate and the departure converts a default into a decision.

He steelmans the opposition before he answers it. Nearly every piece contains a section called "The honest counterargument" or "The fair objection," where he states the other side better than it usually states itself. In **The Wall That Didn't Hold** he grants that an index is supposed to reflect the market as it is, not as a committee wishes it were, and that curating the index swaps a transparent rule for someone's judgment. In **The Trustee Who Drained a Trust to [figure withheld: see the cited source and the live register]** he acknowledges that courts do sometimes weigh ability to pay and that a penalty no one can collect deters no one already ruined. He answers those objections, but he never pretends they are frivolous, which makes the answer harder to dismiss.

He treats protection and control as currencies you trade, not benefits you stack. **The Wall That Didn't Hold** and **The trust nobody funded** both show that the structure only works if you genuinely give up what the structure says you gave up. Retained control means retained exposure. A revocable trust does not protect assets from creditors under NCGS 36C-5-505 because revocable means you kept control, and keeping control means keeping the risk. An irrevocable trust with removal power and investment authority still in the grantor's hands is irrevocable in name and revocable in fact. The families who want both total control and total protection are asking for a wall with a door they keep the key to, and courts have started noticing the key.

He refuses to let professional limits become ethical cover. **Who Takes the Trust Nobody Gets Rich On?** distinguishes between thin margins, which are fair to name, and thin margins as a reason to decline the work, which are not. A fiduciary duty was never conditioned on the account being lucrative, and the reason the role carries legal weight instead of just a service agreement is that someone answers for what belongs to a person who cannot fully answer for themselves. Naming a limit is honesty; hiding behind it is something else.

He learned the discipline in uniform and he keeps explaining trust law through that lens. **A Fiduciary Mindset** traces property accountability in the 82nd Airborne, where signing for equipment meant you answered for it with documentation and your signature meant something, to trust administration, where a trustee holds legal title to property that belongs in every meaningful sense to someone else. The system has to work when you are not in the room, risk is managed in advance rather than apologized for afterward, and the vulnerable get the most care. He does not argue the military taught him trust law; he argues it taught him the posture trust law assumes you already have.

## Where he has repeated himself

He has now circled the gap between statutory duty and industry practice three times: once on remaindermen owed information they never receive, once on life expectancy assumptions no one examines, and once on special needs trusts no one wants to administer. The unwritten essay is about what compliance culture actually measures. He keeps showing that the industry discharges duties at the minimum because no one checks, and the minimum is where trust erodes. The through line is that a duty satisfied on paper but not in fact is the operational definition of a system that works for the trustee and not for the beneficiary. The piece would be called something like "The Duty Discharged and the Duty Done" and it would force the question: if no beneficiary complains and no regulator sanctions you, but the statute said you owed more, did you actually comply?

He has written the funding essay twice, once in detail in **The trust nobody funded** and once in passing in **The Wall That Didn't Hold**. The repetition suggests the next version is not another explanation of how to fund a trust but a harder essay on why attorneys let clients leave without funding and what that says about the economic model of estate planning. The unasked question in both pieces is whether an estate plan sold as a product rather than a relationship is structurally incapable of ensuring the second step happens, because the second step has no closing and no one gets paid for the follow-up call two years later.

The military discipline has appeared in three pieces now as both frame and evidence: the property accountability section in **A Fiduciary Mindset**, the equipment recovery story in the same piece, and the "newest soldier gets the most care" principle in **Who Takes the Trust Nobody Gets Rich On?** and again in **A Fiduciary Mindset**. The unwritten version peels that further back and asks what civilian fiduciary practice would look like if it adopted a military accountability standard wholesale: serial numbers for every asset, change of custody documented every time, random audits by someone outside the chain, and immediate suspension if the count does not clear. It would be called something like "The Hand Receipt Standard" and it would be the most uncomfortable thing he has written, because the answer is that trust administration would look almost nothing like it does now.

## Tension and contradiction

**The Relationship the Statute Already Requires** argues that a trustee owes remaindermen more contact than annual statements provide, and warns that too much contact with heirs could let a business goal color a fiduciary judgment, but it does not define where the line actually is. The tension is between "the statute drew the line well past where most institutions are standing" and "a trust officer who treats every heir as a prospect will eventually compromise independence," and the piece names both without specifying what satisfies the duty without crossing into advocacy. A reader asking what to do Monday morning with the adult child of an income beneficiary would not know from this document alone.

**The Age Your Plan Assumes You Die** holds that a trustee must consider a client-specific life expectancy estimate and cannot discharge impartiality with an unexamined software default, but **The trust nobody funded** warns that retitling a retirement account into a trust has real tax consequences and is never a do it yourself decision. Both pieces insist on specificity over defaults, but the retirement account section pulls back from the same specificity it elsewhere demands, and the only reconciliation offered is "ask before you touch it." The two positions are not contradictory but they sit uneasily together: the life expectancy piece treats individualized estimates as a discharge of duty, and the retirement account section treats individualization without counsel as malpractice.

## What is unsettled

**The Relationship the Statute Already Requires** predicts that banks winning the wealth transfer will win because the children already knew who to call, but it does not answer whether the industry can make that shift without changing the fee model that makes small trusts uneconomical. The statutory duty runs to remaindermen now, but the business case for building relationships with people who are not yet clients assumes the trust survives long enough to pay for the investment. If the income beneficiary lives three years instead of ten, the relationship work costs more than the trust will ever earn, and the piece does not say whether that is a cost the industry will bear or a duty it will continue to discharge on paper and ignore in fact.

**The Age Your Plan Assumes You Die** argues that a conservative life expectancy assumption is defensible if the reasoning is documented, but does not specify how conservative is too conservative or whether the 90th percentile mentioned in Ko's piece is the outer limit. A trustee planning to the 95th percentile for a beneficiary whose health profile points to the 60th would still be acting conservatively, but at some distance from the estimate the conservatism starts to look like an allocation favoring remaindermen, and the piece does not mark where that line is. The unresolved question is whether there is a principled limit to how far a trustee can depart from the client-specific estimate before the departure itself becomes a breach of impartiality.

**The Wall That Didn't Hold** establishes that retained control defeats asset protection but does not define control with enough precision to draft around. Removal power and an investment advisory role were enough to pierce the trust in C.S. v. R.H., but the piece does not say whether removal power alone would have been enough, or whether a grantor serving as co-trustee with an independent institution would survive the test. The rule is genuine relinquishment, but the line between influence and control is still being drawn case by case, and this document does not tell a planner how much latitude a client can keep.
